items.rule: A prime number greater than 1 has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
items.example: 13\text{ is prime because its only positive factors are }1\text{ and }13

items.rule: Every integer greater than 1 can be written uniquely as a product of prime numbers, apart from the order of the factors.
Divisibility by 2 depends on the last digit; divisibility by 5 depends on the last digit being 0 or 5; divisibility by 10 requires the last digit to be 0.
items.formula: 2\mid n\implies\text{last digit even},\quad5\mid n\implies\text{last digit }0\text{ or }5,\quad10\mid n\implies\text{last digit }0

items.rule: A number is divisible by 3 or 9 according to the sum of its digits.
A number is divisible by 4 when its last two digits form a number divisible by 4.
Double the last digit, subtract it from the number formed by the remaining digits, and repeat if useful. Divisibility by 7 is preserved.
items.formula: n=10a+b\implies n\text{ divisible by }7\iff a-2b\text{ divisible by }7

items.rule: A number is divisible by 8 when its last three digits form a number divisible by 8.
Take the alternating sum of digits. If the result is 0 or a multiple of 11, the number is divisible by 11.
items.formula: 11\mid n\iff\text{alternating digit sum is a multiple of }11

items.rule: The Highest Common Factor is the greatest positive integer that divides every given number.
The Least Common Multiple is the smallest positive integer that is a multiple of every given number.
For two positive integers, the product of HCF and LCM equals the product of the two numbers.
Parity tells whether an integer is even or odd and allows many conclusions without fully calculating.

concepts.title: 1. Primes & Factorisation Trees
concepts.subtitle: Breaking Numbers into Prime Building Blocks
concepts.summary: Prime factorisation expresses a composite number as a product of primes. A factor tree repeatedly splits composite factors until every leaf is prime.

points.text: Prime: A number greater than 1 with exactly two positive factors.
Composite: A number greater than 1 with more than two positive factors.
Factor Tree: Keep splitting composite factors until only primes remain.
Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: The prime factorisation of an integer greater than 1 is unique apart from the order of the prime factors.

concepts.trap: Do not stop a factor tree at a composite factor such as 12 or 15. Every final branch must be prime.

concepts.title: 2. Divisibility Rules 2–11
concepts.subtitle: Fast Tests Without Long Division
concepts.summary: Divisibility rules provide efficient tests for common divisors. The most useful tests depend on the last digit, last two or three digits, digit sum, alternating digit sum, or a special transformation.

points.text: 2, 5, 10: Use the last digit.
3, 9: Use the sum of the digits.
4, 8: Use the last two or three digits.
11: Use the alternating sum of digits.
7: Double the last digit and subtract it from the remaining leading part.

concepts.trap: Do not confuse the rules for 3 and 9 with the rules for 4 and 8. Digit sums are for 3 and 9; trailing digits are for 4 and 8.

concepts.title: 3. HCF: Meaning & Finding
concepts.subtitle: The Greatest Shared Factor
concepts.summary: The HCF is the greatest factor common to all given numbers. Prime factorisation gives it by taking the smallest exponent of every prime common to all numbers.

points.text: Meaning: HCF is the greatest positive integer that divides every given number.
Prime-Factor Method: Select only common primes and use their minimum exponents.
Listing Method: List factors or multiples when the numbers are small enough for a quick direct comparison.
Two-Number Check: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers.

concepts.trap: For HCF, take minimum exponents, not maximum exponents. Maximum exponents belong to LCM.

concepts.title: 4. LCM: Meaning & Finding
concepts.subtitle: The First Shared Multiple
concepts.summary: The LCM is the smallest positive multiple common to all given numbers. In prime factorisation, use every prime that appears and take its largest exponent.

points.text: Meaning: LCM is the least positive integer divisible by every given number.
Prime-Factor Method: Include every prime appearing in any factorisation and use its maximum exponent.
Listing Method: Compare multiples until the first common multiple is found.
Connection: For two positive integers, HCF × LCM = product of the numbers.

concepts.trap: For LCM, do not omit a prime that occurs in only one number. Every prime appearing in either factorisation may be needed.

concepts.title: 5. Even/Odd Parity Laws for Proof
concepts.subtitle: Classifying Results Without Full Computation
concepts.summary: Represent even integers as 2k and odd integers as 2k+1. This algebraic representation turns parity statements into short proofs.

points.text: Even + Even: The sum is even.
Odd + Odd: The sum is even.
Even × Odd: The product is even.
Odd × Odd: The product is odd.
Proof Language: Write even numbers as $2m$ and $2n$, and odd numbers as $2m+1$ and $2n+1$.

concepts.trap: Do not say a result is even merely because it 'looks even'. Use the factor 2 or an algebraic parity representation when proving a statement.
